content: 1. The most effective intervention for the primary prevention of cervical cancer is prophylactic HPV vaccination administered before exposure to the virus. 2. HPV vaccines are composed of viral capsid proteins that self-assemble into virus-like particles (VLPs). These particles are non-infectious as they lack viral DNA, essentially functioning as empty shells. 3. Four types of HPV vaccines have been developed: monovalent (targeting HPV 16), bivalent (targeting HPV 16 and 18), quadrivalent (targeting HPV 16, 18, 6, and 11), and nonavalent (targeting HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58). All except the monovalent vaccine are licensed for use. 4. These vaccines stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies against high-risk HPV (hrHPV) types, thereby promoting an immune response. 5. The cancer-preventive effect of HPV vaccines is achieved by preventing persistent hrHPV infections, which are known to lead to high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), both of which are precancerous conditions that can progress to cervical cancer. 6. Clinical trials have demonstrated that three-dose regimens of the monovalent, bivalent, and quadrivalent vaccines are effective in preventing precancerous conditions and persistent hrHPV infections in females aged 15 to 26 years, with no significant increase in serious adverse events. 7. After five to eight years of vaccination, the prevalence of HPV 16 and 18 decreased by 83% in girls aged 13 to 19 years and by 66% in women aged 20 to 24 years, providing strong evidence of the vaccines' effectiveness. 8. A 2020 study showed a significant reduction in cervical cancer incidence in populations with high HPV vaccine uptake, particularly among individuals vaccinated during early adolescence. 9. A systematic review highlighted that two-dose regimens of the bivalent, quadrivalent, and nonavalent vaccines provide immunity equivalent to three-dose regimens. Antibody responses were stronger when the interval between the two doses was six to 12 months. 10. The quadrivalent vaccine offers similar protection to the nonavalent vaccine in reducing the incidence of high-grade CIN, AIS, and cervical cancer in individuals aged 9 to 26 years. Additionally, it has been shown to reduce the incidence of external genital lesions in boys aged 10 to 26 years. 11. Many countries have implemented HPV immunization programs. In the UK, HPV vaccination is part of the routine immunization schedule for boys and girls aged 9 to 13 years. 12. HPV vaccines are effective in preventing hrHPV infections in individuals who have not been previously exposed to the virus. However, they are ineffective in individuals with pre-existing HPV infections, who remain at risk of developing cervical cancer. 13. Secondary prevention methods, such as screening for hrHPV nucleic acids and detecting abnormal or precancerous cellular changes, remain essential for reducing cervical cancer risks. 14. Persistent infection with hrHPV is the primary cause of cervical cancer, with studies estimating that HPV is present in 99.7% of cervical cancer cases worldwide. 15. Other risk factors for cervical cancer include smoking, early age at first sexual intercourse, multiple sexual partners, the presence of other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), and compromised immune status. 16. Individuals receiving immunosuppressive therapy for organ transplants or those infected with HIV are at a higher risk of developing precancerous conditions. 17. Primary prevention strategies for cervical cancer focus on reducing known risk factors through vaccination, smoking cessation, and promoting safer sexual behaviors. 18. Cervical screening aims to detect and treat precancerous conditions early, thereby preventing the progression to invasive cervical cancer.
